messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Nguyen is a 72-year-old man who came to therapy at the urging of his wife, after months of growing tension between them and a near-miss at work that left him shaken. For forty years he had worked as a nanny, first for his own children and later for other families, quietly building a reputation as a patient, gentle caretaker. But in the past year, that patience had begun to fray in ways he could not control.

The event that haunted him had happened nearly fifty years ago, in a small apartment he had shared with his partner at the time. He could still feel the cold linoleum floor against his back, the way his partner’s weight pressed his shoulders down, the repeated impact of a fist against his ribs. It happened in the dark. The bedroom light had burned out a week before, and his partner had refused to replace it. That night, after an argument about money, Minh had been shoved to the floor, and then it was all shadow and pain. He had not fought back. He had not cried out. He had simply lain there, frozen, until it stopped, and then he had gotten up, washed his face, and gone to bed. He never told anyone. He never raised his voice again.

In the decades that followed, Minh built a life around that silence. He married a kind woman who wondered why he never argued, why he turned away from any hint of confrontation, why he insisted on sleeping with a nightlight even though he claimed not to be afraid of the dark. He became a nanny because it let him focus on the needs of others, on routines that were predictable and soft. He learned to suppress any flicker of anger before it surfaced, certain that if he ever let it out, something terrible would happen. When a toddler threw a tantrum, he breathed slowly and walked away. When a parent criticized his work, he nodded and changed nothing. He avoided any situation that might become stressful—parties where politics might come up, phone calls from the building manager about repairs, even conversations with his wife about their adult children’s choices.

He also began to avoid darkness with a thoroughness that bordered on ritual. If the sun set while he was out, he hurried home. In the home where he nannied, he made sure the nursery nightlight was always on before he put the baby down. One evening, while he was rocking the baby in a dim room, the lights flickered and died. The baby was safe, but Minh’s body reacted before his mind could catch up. He found himself on the floor, arms crossed over his chest, exactly as he had lain as a young man, his heart pounding and his breath gone. The terror that had been locked in that memory came flooding back—not as a memory, but as a living thing. It felt as though it belonged to someone else, a stranger whose body had briefly occupied his own. He could not explain to the alarmed mother why he was trembling on the carpet. He simply said, “I need to go home.”

After that, the startle became worse. A sudden movement from a child running toward him made him flinch as if struck. The sound of a door slamming made him drop whatever he held. He could not relax anywhere. At home, he sat rigid in his armchair, eyes scanning the room, waiting for something that never came. His wife noticed that he no longer slept through the night, that he checked the locks three times, that he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind.

What eventually brought him to the clinic was the fear that he would lose his job. The family he worked for had been understanding so far, but they had started to ask questions. He was terrified that if they knew the truth—that he was afraid of the dark, that he could not control his body when a memory rose—they would see him as unstable, unsuitable for caring for their child. He was even more terrified that one day he would react to a sudden movement by pushing a toddler away, by shouting, by becoming what he had spent his whole life trying not to be. He came to therapy hoping for a way to quiet his body, to stop the flinch, to let his wife sleep beside him without him lying awake, rigid and mute, in the dark.
